title: Connecting the Motoko Backend to our JS Frontend
section: 38. Build Your First Defi (Decentralised Finance) DApp - DBANK
summary: Builds the JavaScript that connects the DBank page to the Motoko canister: importing the generated declarations, awaiting canister calls, handling the form submit, converting input strings to floats, guarding against empty inputs, disabling the button during slow update calls, and finally refactoring into one update function.

concepts.heading: Importing the canister into the frontend
points: Import the canister object with a named import from the generated declarations folder, using a relative path (up out of the frontend src folder, into declarations, then the backend canister's folder). Example name: dbank_backend (the lecture's older project calls it dbank).

The declarations folder is generated by dfx. It contains the Candid-derived interface that tells JavaScript which public functions the Motoko actor exposes and what argument types they take. It acts as the bridge between the two languages.
Once imported, canister methods are called like ordinary async functions: checkBalance(), topUp()/topUP(), withdraw(), compound().

concepts.heading: Showing the balance on page load
points: Goal: replace the placeholder number in span#value with the real currentValue whenever the page opens. checkBalance is a query function so it answers quickly.
Register a window event listener for the page-load event. A first test with console.log (check the browser Console tab after a reload) proves the listener fires; then replace the log.
Fetch the balance into a const, grab span#value with document.getElementById and assign its innerText.

Bug seen first: the page displays '[object Promise]'. Canister calls return Promises because the answer arrives asynchronously from the blockchain. Fix: make the callback an async function and put await in front of the canister call so the code pauses until the value arrives.
The raw float has many decimals. Challenge: show only two. Solution: Math.round(value * 100) / 100 (scale up, round to an integer, scale back down).

(Extra) The reference code uses the DOMContentLoaded event instead of load. DOMContentLoaded fires when the HTML is parsed, without waiting for images, so it triggers a bit earlier. Either works here.

concepts.heading: Handling the form submit
points: Select the form with document.querySelector('form'). Selector rules mirror CSS: # for ids, . for classes, bare name for tags.
Attach a 'submit' listener. It fires when the submit input is clicked (or Enter pressed in a field). Make the callback async and accept the event parameter.

Test first with a console.log. It flashes and vanishes, because the form's default behaviour is to submit and reload the page. Calling event.preventDefault() at the top stops that, so fields stay filled and the page does not refresh.
Read the two inputs with document.getElementById('input-amount').value and document.getElementById('withdrawal-amount').value (names chosen: inputAmount, outputAmount, to avoid withdraw typos).

concepts.heading: Type conversion: strings to Float
points: Calling topUp with the raw input value fails with an 'Invalid float64 argument' style error. The generated declarations state the Motoko function takes a Float (64-bit floating point), but an input's .value is a string.
Wrap values in parseFloat() to convert them to numbers before sending. The inputs already carry step='0.01' so decimals up to cents are accepted.
After conversion the call succeeds silently. The page does not refresh yet, so the balance span has to be updated again by repeating the checkBalance-and-display lines after the calls.
Test: top up by 10 and watch the displayed balance move from e.g. 1446 to 1456.

concepts.heading: Giving feedback during slow update calls
points: Update calls (non-query) go through consensus and take roughly 2-3 seconds. With no feedback users click repeatedly, sending duplicate transactions.
Select the submit button from the event: event.target.querySelector('#submit-btn'). event.target is the form that fired submit.
Before the calls: button.setAttribute('disabled', true). After the balance refresh: button.removeAttribute('disabled').
Do not use setAttribute('disabled', false). A boolean attribute disables the element whenever it is present, regardless of value, so it must be removed instead.
The #submit-btn:disabled CSS from the previous lecture dims the button so the user sees it is locked.
After finishing, reset the field with input.value = '' so the old amount is not left behind.

concepts.heading: Guarding against empty inputs
points: Because the single submit handler serves both fields, an empty field would still be passed on: parseFloat('') is NaN, which corrupts the stored balance (the Debug print on the backend showed nan).
Fix used in the lecture: wrap the top-up call in an if that checks the field's value string has length not equal to 0. Only then call topUp.

The withdrawal part is a student task: add a second, separate if for withdrawal-amount with the same length check, await withdraw(outputAmount), then clear that input. Two separate ifs are used (not else-if) so both a top-up and a withdrawal can happen in one submit; a plain else would be wrong.
(Extra) The reference repo guards with !isNaN(parseFloat(...)) instead of checking string length. Both prevent sending NaN; the isNaN version also rejects non-numeric text.
Tip given: copy and paste ids and function names to avoid typos like withdrawl.

concepts.heading: Adding compound interest and resetting canister state
points: Call compound() after the top-up/withdraw block so interest is applied every time the user transacts, then refresh the displayed balance.
The backend rate is intentionally huge (a fraction of a percent per elapsed second), so the balance grows visibly quickly during a demo; real interest would be far smaller.

Bad input corrupted the stored state, so the backend was reset. The stable variables only reinitialise reliably if the code actually changes between deploys. Procedure: comment out the lines that set currentValue and startTime, run dfx deploy, then uncomment them (currentValue back to 300) and deploy again. A Debug.print confirms the value.
To restart cleanly: Ctrl+C the npm and dfx processes, then run dfx start, dfx deploy, npm start again.

concepts.heading: Refactor into a single update function
points: The check-balance-and-display lines appear twice (on load and after a transaction). Extract them into one async function (called updateBalance in the reference, update in the lecture) and call it from both places.
The next lecture lists likely errors; skip it if everything worked.

task.name: Wire the DBank frontend to the Motoko canister
task.starting_point: The 38.08 project: HTML, CSS and logo in place, empty JS entry file, working Motoko actor with topUp, withdraw, checkBalance and compound.
task.goal: A page that shows the live balance, tops up and withdraws via the form, compounds interest on each transaction, and locks the button while waiting.
steps: On page load, await checkBalance() and write the number into span#value.
Challenge: round to two decimals with Math.round(x * 100) / 100.
Add a submit listener on the form; call event.preventDefault().
Read both inputs and convert them with parseFloat.
Disable the submit button, then call topUp when the top-up field is filled.
Challenge: add a separate if that calls withdraw when the withdrawal field is filled.
Call compound(), refresh the balance, clear both inputs, and remove the disabled attribute.
Refactor the repeated balance-refresh lines into one async function.
task.expected_result: Typing 10 in the top-up box and submitting raises the balance by about 10 plus a little interest after a 2-3 second wait; withdrawing lowers it; empty boxes cause no NaN.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 38 - Build Your First Defi (Decentralised Finance) DApp - DBANK/38.09 Connecting the Motoko Backend to our JS Frontend/Dbank/src/dbank_frontend/src/main.js

pitfalls: Forgetting await: the page shows [object Promise] instead of a number.
Sending the input's string value to a Float parameter causes an invalid argument error; use parseFloat.
Empty fields yield NaN and corrupt the canister's stored balance.
Using setAttribute('disabled', false) does not re-enable a button; remove the attribute.
Using else instead of a second if prevents correct handling of separate fields.
Stable variables may not reset after a small code change; comment out, deploy, restore, deploy again.
Typos in function names such as topUP vs topUp (the reference backend spells it topUP, so the frontend call must match whatever the actor declares).
Reference repo quirk: it keeps the author's NaN guard and capitalised topUP; the lecture's own code used a string-length check.

playground.coverage: No playground lesson yet (the playground only has files for sections 1-11, 14, 15).
gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Talking to a backend from a form': blurb on async calls, Promises and why await is needed.

Tasks: (1) show a fake balance on load using await on a mock function, (2) round to two decimals, (3) intercept submit with preventDefault, (4) parseFloat and skip empty fields, (5) disable and re-enable the button around a delayed call.
Starter code idea: a mock 'canister' object whose methods return Promises resolved after setTimeout(2500).
Interactive demo idea: toggle checkboxes for 'await', 'preventDefault', 'parseFloat', 'removeAttribute' and show what breaks on submit (object Promise, page reload, NaN, stuck disabled button).
